hypothesis: A matrix product with fewer than about 8 activation rows is limited by streaming its weights from DRAM; the engine routine as shipped (single core below 16 rows) is predicted at 12.0 ms for one encoder layer and the eight-core split at 3.2 to 4 ms.
prediction:
A matrix product with R activation rows reads each int8 weight byte once and uses it for R multiply-accumulates, so with R below about 8 the weight bytes stream at close to one byte per useful multiply-accumulate. The packed 8-bit weight by 16-bit activation kernel of the speech engine (a four-row, eight-channel tile of dot-product instructions) computes four rows per tile whatever R is, so a tile with R below 4 does the work of four rows. The engine's measurement of the eight-core kernel is 30.4 giga multiply-accumulates per second on full tiles; the engine's worker weights (1024 for an A76 core, about 305 for an A55 core) place one A76 core at 8.0 giga multiply-accumulates per second.
The benchmark times one pass over the twelve weight matrices of one encoder layer of a 0.6-billion-parameter streaming recognizer (23 MiB, 24.1 million bytes) and over one 0.5 MiB matrix called 64 times (weights resident in the L2 and L3 caches), with two kernels: the engine's linear routine as shipped (calling core alone when R is below 16) and the same dot-product tile with the output channels split over all eight cores, each weight tile reused for all row groups. Predicted time per pass from tile counts of ceil(R/4) four-row groups, the rates above and, for the streaming stack, a floor of 24.1 MB divided by 8.4 to 12.7 GB/s (2.0 to 2.9 ms), in ms (as shipped streaming / split streaming / split resident): R=1 12.0 / 3.2 to 4 / 4.4; R=2 12.0 / 3.2 to 4 / 4.4; R=7 24.0 / 6.4 to 7 / 8.8; R=14 48.0 / 12.7 to 14 / 17.5; R=64 51 / 51 to 56 / 70. At R = 1 and 2 the split-kernel prediction is set by the padded tiles, not by the memory, so the streaming rate in multiply-accumulates per second should equal the resident rate within about 25 percent; a streaming rate further below shows a limit from the memory.
Dispatch cost and in-cache rate of the split kernel: the pass times at one and two rows lie close to the time that the streamed bytes need at the all-eight read rate (24.1 MB at 8.4 GB/s is 2.9 ms), which suggests a memory limit, but each call dispatches seven worker tasks and the padded tiles take compute time. The in-cache control dispatches once and has each worker repeat its own 64 KiB share of a 512 x 1024 matrix 64 times. The padded-tile rate of the eight cores at 64 rows is the best case, 74.5 giga multiply-accumulates per second (measured with the split kernel in an earlier run); a pass of 64 repeats of the 0.524 million-weight matrix then takes 64 x 0.524 M x 4 padded rows / 74.5 G = 1.8 ms at one or two rows, 3.6 ms at seven rows, 7.2 ms at fourteen rows and 28.8 ms at 64 rows, plus under 0.1 ms for the one dispatch. The streaming pass of twelve calls then holds 1.3 ms of tile compute and about 0.6 ms of dispatch at one row, so a measured streaming time near 3.1 ms leaves about 1.2 ms for the memory.
conclusion: Measured, one encoder layer (twelve matrices, 24.1 MB of int8 weights), median of eight passes, ms (engine routine as shipped / split over eight cores / split with weights resident): R=1 3.72 / 3.07 / 1.57; R=2 3.93 / 3.09 / 1.59; R=7 7.99 / 3.45 / 3.16; R=14 15.38 / 5.33 / 6.50; R=64 28.17 / 20.73 / 27.97. The resident column repeats a 0.5 MiB matrix 64 times, which is 33.5 million weights per pass against 24.1 million for the streaming pass; it is 39 percent more work, and a compute floor for the streaming pass at R = 1, 2 and 7 only after scaling by 0.72. At R = 64 the resident figure is slower than the streaming one because its eight workers share only 64 units of 16 channels. The engine routine as shipped runs below 16 rows on one A76 core and does about 26 giga multiply-accumulates per second of padded tile work, three times the 8 assumed from the worker weights; its single-core times are 3.7 and 3.9 ms at one and two rows, not 12. The 30.4 giga multiply-accumulates per second quoted for the speech engine is the average of its whole linear stage including row quantization and dispatch; the split routine reaches 74 to 85 giga multiply-accumulates per second of padded tile work. The split routine at one and two rows takes 3.07 ms: tile compute 1.1 ms (resident time scaled to the weight count), twelve dispatches 0.65 ms (54 microseconds per call, from the difference between 64 separate calls and one dispatch with 64 repeats), and the remaining 1.3 ms is the memory limit: 24.1 MB in about 2.4 ms of effective streaming is 10 GB/s, between the all-eight rate and the single-A76 rate. At seven rows the pass is still within 10 percent of that limit; from fourteen rows it is compute-bound. The per-core-rate predictions failed (single-core 12 ms predicted, 3.7 ms measured); the memory-limit inference held.

hypothesis: Source analysis: SunstoneOS configures the DRAM path as the vendor does except for nine NSI port words; ranked explanations for the falling aggregate read rate.
prediction:
Pin rate: the board's boot0 selects DRAM parameter set 5, whose clock is 2040 MHz and whose type is LPDDR5 (docs/vendor-firmware/data/boot0-tables.json, dram_parameter_sets). The chip datasheet gives LPDDR4 up to 2133 MHz and LPDDR5 up to 2400 MHz (section on external memory). LPDDR4 at 2133 MHz is the 4266 megatransfer per second part, so the datasheet states the clock as half the data rate, and set 5 runs at 4080 megatransfers per second. dram_tpr13 bit 6 selects two channels and the datasheet gives a 32-bit interface: 4080 million transfers per second on 4 bytes is 16.32 GB/s. The training records store the P-state clocks (2040, 1165, 816 and 408 MHz) and not the mode registers, so the ratio between stated clock and data rate rests on the datasheet convention; a board read of the LPDDR5 mode registers or the controller timing would confirm it. Set 1 of the same table runs at 2400 MHz (19.2 GB/s); the board does not select it and reaching it needs a DRAM clock and voltage change.
Configuration against the vendor's: the boot path runs boot0's board setup and init_DRAM unchanged from the FEL-loaded wrapper (boot/a733/ddr-entry.S), so controller timing, scheduling, page policy, address mapping and training come from the vendor's code and parameter set; no source describes the controller register fields (docs/vendor-firmware/boot-rom-and-boot0.md, open questions), so those items are equal by construction. Table (setting: ours / vendor / source):
- Controller scheduling, page policy, bank and rank interleave, address mapping: boot0 init_DRAM with parameter set 5 / the same code and set / ddr-entry.S calls 0x48fad and 0x49bdd; boot0-tables.json.
- DRAM clock: 2040 MHz (P-state 0) / 2040 MHz for set 5 / dram-fast-boot.md.
- MBUS clock: 600 MHz after EL3 entry / 600 MHz / docs/status/memory-dma.md board-qualified scope; action-plan.md item 12.
- NSI port words 0x02023a14, 0x02023c14, 0x02023e14, 0x02024014, 0x02024214, 0x0202446c, 0x0202466c, 0x0202200c, 0x0202220c: not written (before the boot-path adoption) / 0x3f, 0x7f, 0xf, 0xf1, 0xf1, 0x40a05, 0x40a05, 1, 1 / boot0 routine 0x48f38 called from 0x49050 after init_DRAM; the FEL wrapper skipped it; the SCP writes the same values on resume (scp-firmware.md step 9).
- NSI initiator ports for DE, IOMMU and the other masters (priority, mode, select): not written, reset values / Linux sunxi_set_nsi_qos_params writes DE priority 2 and IOMMU priority 3 / dram-bus-priority.md; the CPU is not an NSI port master (dram-controller.md).
- CPU to DRAM path: direct channels that no NSI port counts / the same / dram-controller.md.
- DSU and L3 clock: 1274 MHz at 1000 mV, the vendor's top point / 780 MHz left by boot0, the shipped kernel builds no dsufreq driver, the vendor table's top point is 1274 MHz / cpu-top-opp.md; board-kernel-config; sunxi-dsufreq.c.
- DSU auxiliary control (CLUSTERACTLR_EL1): erratum values for the DSU revision, bit 15 and bits 16:15 when selected by the revision / not written by the vendor monitor (DSU errata reported, not compiled) / platform/a733/cpu_coherence.c; tf-a-monitor.md.
- CLUSTERECTLR_EL1: reset value / reset value (the vendor monitor never writes it) / reference-backsolve-cpu.md errata paragraph.
- A55 CPUECTLR_EL1 (L1 prefetch limit L1PCTL, reset 5 outstanding, and L3 prefetch distance L3PCTL): reset value, except revision 0 with no L3 / reset value / A55 TRM CPUECTLR; cpu_coherence.c line 27; reference-backsolve-cpu.md.
- A76 CPUECTLR_EL1 (PF_DIS hardware prefetch reset enabled, single-stride L2 distance reset 40 lines, DRAM prefetch hints PFT_LS reset off): reset value for r4p1 / reset value / A76 r4p1 TRM; cpu_coherence.c lines 39 and 40 apply only up to r2p0 and r3p0.
- A76 CPUACTLR2_EL1 (the board's A76 cores are r4p1, MIDR 0x414fd0b1): bits 0, 16 and 22 (errata 2356586 and 3888013 and the static speculative-store-bypass control); CPUACTLR_EL1 bit 13 and CPUACTLR2_EL1 bit 2 apply only up to r4p0 and are not set / only erratum 1946160 (system registers, not these bits); the dynamic speculative-store-bypass control clears bit 16 / cpu_coherence.c lines 31 to 38; reference-backsolve-cpu.md row 'A76 reset errata'; docs/hardware/a733-facts.md; the bit meanings are reserved in the TRM.
- DRAM temperature derating: not applied, DDR at 40 to 45 degrees Celsius / not applied below the trip / dram-controller.md.
Two differences from the vendor remained: (1) the vendor's NSI words were not written in our boot path (their ports 29 to 35 lie beyond the 21 initiator ports of enum nsi_pmu for this chip, ports 32 and 33 are target agents on the way to the DRAM controller; boot0 and the SCP both write them; the field meaning is undocumented; the action plan listed three of the nine words as not written by boot0, the routine at 0x48f38 writes all nine); (2) the A76 auxiliary control bits are an addition of ours (meaning reserved in the TRM except bit 16, the speculative-store-bypass control; the streaming loop issues no stores, so bit 16 has no work to slow; the other bits are unexplained). Neither the prefetchers (reset values at both levels) nor the DSU clock differ.
Benchmark check of apps/dram-bandwidth: each core reads its own contiguous 5 MiB slice of a 40 MiB buffer at multiples of 5 MiB from the base (the base address was not recorded, so page alignment as seen by the controller was not shown; the buffer exceeds the 1 MiB L3 by 40); cores start at a barrier; the result held only the pass duration and not each core's time, so with a fixed amount of work per core the faster cores finish first and the all-eight aggregate (bytes over the slowest core's time) is lower than the rate while all cores read; two equal A76 cores or six equal A55 cores are not affected in the same way. apps/dram-scaling replaces the pass with a fixed 12 ms window per variant, every core streams until the window ends and reports chunks read and time to its last chunk; the decoder reports the rate per core, the sum of those rates, and the bytes over the slowest core's time; the result records the buffer base address.
Ranked hypotheses for the falling total (rank, hypothesis, why, separating prediction):
1. Independent sequential streams lose row-buffer hits and bank parallelism in the controller. Why: one stream reaches 78 percent of the pin rate, two equal A76 streams 70 percent, six A55 streams 55 percent, so the loss grows with the number of streams; scheduling and mapping equal the vendor's. Separation: the all-core sum changes when streams are staggered by a bank or row amount, and falls further when a core issues two or more streams (mode 2) or page-sized strides (mode 3); a flat result across staggers excludes it.
2. The interconnect words that the vendor writes after DRAM initialization change arbitration towards the controller. Why: absent in our boot path, present in the vendor's, and ports 32 and 33 are the controller's target agents. Separation: a board read of the nine words shows whether reset values differ; a write of the vendor values then shows the effect on the all-core sum (needs approval).
3. The all-eight and six-core figures understate the rate while all cores read (equal work per core, different core speeds, a tail with fewer readers). Separation: the sum of per-core rates in the fixed window exceeds the earlier figure by more than 10 percent for all eight cores and by less than 3 percent for six A55 cores.
4. A limit on outstanding transactions of the DSU or cluster interface, with prefetch traffic fetched and evicted before use (six A55 cores prefetch up to 5 lines each at L1 and deeper at L3 into a 128 KiB private L2 and a shared 1 MiB L3). Separation: a plateau instead of a fall (per-core rate falls as 1/n beyond a core count, total flat); the 4 KiB chunk variants (modes 1 to 3) reset the stride detector at every chunk and reduce prefetch depth, so a higher total there points to prefetch waste.
5. Placement of the buffer across banks and ranks through the base address alignment (unknown base, unknown mapping). Separation: the stagger variants and the recorded base address.
6. MBUS or DRAM clock below the assumed value, or refresh derating. Excluded by the records: MBUS reads 600 MHz after EL3 entry on both boards, DDR is at 40 to 45 degrees Celsius, and one A76 core reaches 78 percent of the pin rate on the same clocks.
The performance monitor counters and controller counters were not available to the first application: its tasks run at EL0 where the counters trap (docs/cpu-pmu.md), and no source documents the controller registers.
Scaling image plan: one image runs 32 variants on port 3-1 in development DRAM mode at CPU-L 1794 MHz, CPU-B 2002 MHz, DSU 1274 MHz: core sets of one, two, four and six A55 cores, one and two A76 cores, four A55 with both A76, and all eight; stagger offsets 4 KiB, 64 KiB and 256 KiB (core c starts c times the stagger into a 1 MiB window of its slot) for six A55, two A76 and eight cores; the access patterns of modes 1 to 3 for one A55, one A76, six A55, two A76 and eight cores. Each variant reads one warm-up window and three timed windows of 12 ms.
conclusion: Source analysis only; the board runs it prescribes are the scaling and interconnect records (1793600409082394041-436818e2, 1793600534434449836-8f1652a3, 1793600624723356256-fb710c2d, 1793601413670925677-13bb2fa0 and the later runs in memory-dma.jsonl). Cause as established by them: the evidence supports hypothesis 1 (loss of row-buffer and bank locality when several independent streams reach the controller) with these limits. The controller is configured by boot0's code and parameter set, so its scheduling, page policy and address mapping equal the vendor's, and a vendor kernel on the same board meets the same loss with eight independent streams. The A76 and A55 prefetchers, the DSU clock and the MBUS clock equal the vendor's or its top point, and the loss does not respond to the software-prefetch variant. The one difference from the vendor that remained, the nine NSI words, was tested later and is not a cause. The loss is a property of the memory system under many independent streams, not a SunstoneOS configuration error that the data identifies. No counter in the sources held observes row hits or bank conflicts, so hypothesis 1 is supported by exclusion and by the address dependence, not proven; a proof needs the controller register documentation or a trace of the controller's own counters.
narrative: Source and datasheet analysis of the memory configuration, no board run. It derives the 16.32 GB/s pin rate, compares SunstoneOS settings with the vendor's, checks the first benchmark and ranks six explanations of the falling aggregate rate; the board runs it prescribes are the scaling, interconnect and counter records in memory-dma.jsonl.

hypothesis: Per-port quality-of-service settings of the NSI bound the CPU worst-case memory latency under NPU, camera and DMA load.
prediction:
The boot path leaves every initiator port at the same priority, so a long NPU or camera burst queues CPU reads behind it in the controller. The vendor driver (sunxi-nsi.c, sunxi-nsi.h) exposes these knobs per initiator port n at 0x02020000 + 0x200 * n; their effect is predicted from the driver and the common meaning of the terms, not measured. Knob, register, vendor use, prediction for CPU worst-case latency under DMA load:
- Priority of a port: +0x14 bits 3:0, two 2-bit fields, set to p from 0 to 3; vendor DE 2, IOMMU 3. Raising the CPU ports (19, 20) above the NPU, camera and DMA ports lets CPU requests win arbitration at the NSI. Bounds the queueing delay behind a competing burst to roughly one request of the other master per arbitration point, but does not shorten the queue already inside the DRAM controller.
- High-priority read class: +0xc (bit 16 on this chip) through nsi_port_sethpr; boot0 writes 1 at +0xc of the ISP and CSI ports. Moves a port's reads to the controller's high-priority queue if the bit has that meaning. Documented only by the function name; test on one port before relying on it.
- Absolute bandwidth limit: +0x28 with +0x2c (saturation), enabled through nsi_port_set_abs_bwlen; none in the device tree. Caps a streaming master (NPU, ISP, CSI, video) to a bandwidth share, bounding how much of the controller's queue it can occupy; the most direct way to bound CPU latency against a master whose traffic is known, at the cost of that master's throughput.
- Port mode: +0x10 bits 1:0; 0 for DE and IOMMU. Meaning not documented; leave at 0.
- Input/output select: +0x18 bit 0; 1 for DE and IOMMU. Meaning not documented; leave at 1.
- Target-agent words: +0x14 of ports 29 to 33 and +0x6c of ports 34 and 35; boot0 values 0x3f, 0x7f, 0xf, 0xf1, 0xf1, 0x40a05, 0x40a05. Not documented; they sit on the way to the controller and may carry arbitration at the controller side. The write of boot0's values did not change the CPU-only bandwidth, so the effect, if any, appears only under contention.
- DRAM controller queue and page policy: set by boot0's parameter set, same as ours.
Measurement method: the loaded read latency of a core is its outstanding refills divided by its refill rate, which the Arm counters at EL1 give. Run a fixed CPU read loop on one core while the NPU or a copy engine streams; record the maximum and the 99th percentile of the time per refill with the ports as inherited, then with the CPU priorities raised, then with a bandwidth limit on the streaming master. This needs a second master in the image. The NPU stage and the camera pipeline define the loads that matter; the scheduler stream owns the timing budgets.
conclusion: Not yet run for the NPU, DMA and other masters; only the control (every competitor a CPU port) ran and showed no effect (1793604009213366498-b525353f). Ways to the NPU condition: link the apps/dram-qos EL1 probes (the chase and control functions and the priority job, about 150 lines) into a finite NPU image beside its job stream, which the NPU stream owner must do because it owns those files; or use the GPU as the second master through the compute queue with a streaming-read kernel, which needs a GPU program that the tree does not hold. The decision rule has no data.
narrative: Prediction derived from the vendor NSI driver sources (sunxi-nsi.c, sunxi-nsi.h); no board run. The measuring application apps/dram-qos exists and ran the control conditions (see 1793604009006779744-6a685222 and 1793604009213366498-b525353f).
